heading: Check grant eligibility before writing the application
body:
A funding opportunity is worth pursuing when the applicant, project, geography, timing, and permitted use of funds fit the actual notice. A matching keyword in a directory is a lead for research. The official funder’s notice controls eligibility and application requirements.

Use a short go-or-no-go review

Record the applicant’s legal type, required status, service area, project purpose, eligible costs, matching-fund obligations, deadline, and submission system. Link each answer to the current official notice or an authorized clarification. Mark an unanswered requirement as unresolved rather than treating it as permission.

For a fictional nonprofit considering an equipment grant, confirm whether the program funds purchases, reimbursement after purchase, or another arrangement. Those structures create different cash needs. Also check whether the organization must maintain the equipment or meet reporting obligations after the award. A grant amount is not necessarily cash available when the project starts.

Separate eligibility from competitiveness

An organization can qualify to apply and still have a weak proposal for the program’s priorities. Once eligibility is confirmed, compare the project with the scoring criteria, required evidence, and reporting capacity. Estimate staff time before starting a long application so the board or project owner can make an informed choice.

For federal opportunities, Grants.gov’s eligibility guidance explains applicant categories, and its applicant resources explain the application workflow. Confirm registration and authorized submission access early. Use this directory to find opportunities, then verify current status, dates, and instructions on the official source before applying.
